GPC.text: More than 1,544,000 total outages across its territory after landfall on September 26, 2024 (a running total, not all at once).
More than 523,000 customers restored in the first 48 hours; more than 95% of affected customers (1.3 million+) restored by October 5.
More than 20,000 personnel, including crews from 35+ assisting companies (other states, Canada, Alabama Power and Mississippi Power).
345+ transmission structures rebuilt or repaired, against 12,300+ broken distribution poles and 1,500+ miles of downed lines.

DESC.text: 386,270 customers without power at the peak, on September 27, 2024.
Nearly 100% of affected customers restored by midday October 8.
More than 4,000 crew members, a "14-state army" of lineworkers, tree crews and employee volunteers.
Its field force included 1,565 distribution linemen but only 57 transmission linemen, plus 430 tree contractors.
130 transmission poles and 350 spans of transmission line damaged, against 2,130 distribution poles and 6,840 spans of distribution line.

notes.text: No source found showing Georgia Power and Dominion Energy SC sent crews to each other. Dominion's president said neighboring states were too hard-hit to send help, so crews came from as far as Illinois and Texas.
The simulation's tree-damage scale is tuned so Dominion's expected damaged spans match the 350 it reported, so that match is not an independent check.

DESC.text: About 30,000 customers out at the peak, just before midnight on August 8, 2024, as the storm left; more than 120,000 had outages over the four days.
About 2,000 employees, crew members and contractors, with help from Georgia, Florida, Kentucky and West Virginia.

GPC.text: 132,396 customers without power at 4:30 p.m. on August 30, 2023, while the storm was still passing.

A restoration team of more than 5,500 personnel, with help from Alabama Power and Mississippi Power, restored nearly 200,000 customers by the next day; hardest-hit areas were expected at 95% by September 1-2.

DESC.text: About 29,000 customers out at the storm's peak, around 9 p.m. on August 30, 2023; half were back by midnight.

GPC.text: Only scattered outages: more than 500 customers out in Central Georgia on September 29, 2022 and about 100 in Savannah the next morning.

DESC.text: More than 110,000 customers out at the peak after landfall near Georgetown on September 30, 2022.
Down to about 15,000 in under 18 hours, with the rest expected back by sunset on October 3.
About 2,000 South Carolina-based team members, plus 700 crew members and contractors from Dominion Energy Virginia and contract line workers from South Carolina, Tennessee and Maryland.

GPC.text: About 8,000 customers statewide without power as of 11 a.m. on August 17, 2021, from scattered tree damage.
More than 550,000 customers without power at 7 a.m. on October 29, 2020.
About 798,000 customers restored (more than 97%) by 5:30 p.m. on October 31, and 99% by 1 p.m. on November 2.
More than 4,000 personnel, with help from utilities in 14 states; 700+ broken poles and 3,400+ spans of wire down.

notes.text: In South Carolina, Zeta's outages were mostly in Duke Energy's Upstate territory; no Dominion Energy SC figure was found.

GPC.text: About 28,000 customers without power at 11 a.m. on September 17, 2020; about 88,000 had been restored since midnight and about 9,800 were still out by 5 p.m.
Sent about 500 company and contractor personnel to help Alabama Power.
Nearly 770,000 customers out at the peak on September 11, 2017, by its September 12 count; a day later it said nearly 1 million had initially lost service.
Nearly 8,000 personnel from Georgia Power, other Southern Company utilities and assisting utilities; it targeted 95% of affected customers by Sunday, September 17.
More than 1,000 broken or damaged distribution poles and about 5,000 spans of wire; no transmission figure was given.

DESC.text: SCE&G (now Dominion Energy SC): more than 154,000 customers lost power on September 11, 2017, and all were restored by Friday morning, September 15.

GPC.text: About 338,000 customers lost power on October 7-8, 2016; 99% were back by October 14.
More than 90% restored by October 12, with about 5,000 personnel including crews from Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas.
About 1,000 damaged poles and 3,000 spans of wire (distribution-level figures).

DESC.text: SCE&G (now Dominion Energy SC): about 290,000 customers, 40% of its customers, out at the peak; 90% restored by the afternoon of October 12.
About 2,000 of its own resources plus 1,000 off-system linemen and tree crews.

GPC.text: More than 49,000 customers without power at 10 p.m. on September 2, 2016, down to about 3,500 by 5 a.m. on September 4.
More than 3,000 personnel, including more than 30 crews from Tennessee.
More than 200,000 customers without power on the morning of October 11, 2018.
322,000 customers restored by 4 p.m. on October 12, with more than 5,200 personnel; Albany and Bainbridge were estimated for October 15 and 16.

99%, or more than 385,000 customers, restored by October 19, with more than 5,800 personnel including more than a dozen assisting utilities from as far away as Illinois, New York, Pennsylvania and Texas.
More than 3,500 spans of wire and about 1,000 poles damaged; no separate transmission figure was given.
About 15,000 customers without power at 8 a.m. on September 5, 2019, with nearly 1,500 personnel responding to more than 250 cases of damage.

DESC.text: 274,000 South Carolina customers impacted; 10,600 still out on the afternoon of September 7, 2019, with nearly all targeted for Sunday night, September 8.
About 1,500 outages in the afternoon of August 3, 2020, down to just under 550 by 10:30 p.m.

notes.text: Isaias hit Virginia and North Carolina far harder; Dominion Energy sent available South Carolina crews there.

About 77,000 South Carolina customers were out statewide, across all utilities, as repairs began on September 15, 2018; most damage was in northeast SC, which is served mainly by Duke Energy and Santee Cooper. No SCE&G-only figure was found.

florence.outageCostHidden: The model predicts far more outages for these two utilities than were published for Florence, so a dollar figure would be too high.
